nominative: the 'subject' case — who or what does the action, or what something 'is'
genitive: the 'of' case — possession or belonging (the king's, of the king)
dative: the 'to/for' case — the person or thing something is given to, said to, done for
accusative: the 'object' case — what the action is done to; also where you go to (ad urbem)
ablative: the 'by/with/from' case — means, agent, place where, time when, separation
vocative: the case for calling someone: 'Quīnte!' — same as the nominative except -us → -e
locative: the 'at/in' case for cities, small islands and a few nouns (Rōmae, domī)
masculine: grammatical gender m — not about sex: 'ager' is masculine
neuter: grammatical gender n — neither m nor f; its nominative and accusative are always identical
common gender: a noun that can be masculine or feminine (cīvis = citizen, man or woman)
imperfect: ongoing, repeated or background action in the past: 'I was sending', 'I used to send'
perfect: a completed past action: 'I sent', 'I have sent'
pluperfect: 'had' — past before another past: 'I had sent'
future perfect: 'will have' — done before a future moment: 'I will have sent'
indicative: the plain mood for stating facts and asking direct questions
subjunctive: the mood for wishes, commands reported, purposes, possibilities — often 'may / might / should / were to'
infinitive: the 'to' form: 'to send'; in Latin also 'that … sends' after verbs of saying
participle: a verb used as an adjective: 'sending' (present), 'sent / having been sent' (perfect), 'about to send' (future)
gerund: the verb as a noun: 'sending' (ad nāvigandum = for sailing). Only genitive, dative, accusative, ablative
gerundive: an adjective meaning 'needing to be …-ed': mittendus = 'to be sent'. With esse: 'must be sent'
supine: a verbal noun in -um ('to …', after a verb of motion: 'vēnit dormītum' = came to sleep) or -ū ('to …' after an adjective: 'facile dictū' = easy to say)
active: the subject does the action: 'he sends'
passive: the subject receives the action: 'he is sent'
deponent: looks passive, means active: sequitur = 'he follows', not 'he is followed'
semi-deponent: active in the present system, passive-looking in the perfect: gaudeō 'I rejoice', gāvīsus sum 'I rejoiced'
impersonal: used only in the 3rd person singular with 'it': licet 'it is allowed', decet 'it is fitting'
enclitic: a little word glued onto the end of another: -que 'and', -ne '? (question)', -ve 'or'
declension: the pattern a noun or adjective follows for its case endings. Latin has five
1st declension: nouns in -a, genitive -ae (puella, īnsula); mostly feminine
2nd declension: nouns in -us / -er (masculine) or -um (neuter), genitive -ī (servus, puer, verbum)
3rd declension: the big mixed group, genitive -is (rēx rēgis, corpus corporis, urbs urbis)
i-stem: a 3rd-declension noun with -ium in the genitive plural (and -ia, -ī for neuters): urbs urbium, mare maria
conjugation: the pattern a verb follows. Latin has four, told apart by the infinitive: -āre, -ēre, -ere, -īre
2nd conjugation: infinitive -ēre with a long ē (moneō, monēre)
3rd conjugation: infinitive -ere with a short e (regō, regere); the -iō type adds i: capiō, capere
irregular verb: a verb that does not follow the four conjugations: sum, possum, eō, ferō, volō, nōlō, mālō, fīō
defective verb: a verb missing most of its forms (inquit, ait, ōdī, meminī)
positive: the basic degree of an adjective or adverb: 'big'
pronoun: a word standing in for a noun: he, this, who, I
personal pronoun: I, you, we (ego, tū, nōs, vōs); the 3rd person uses is, ea, id
reflexive: refers back to the subject: sē 'himself / herself / themselves', suus 'his own'
demonstrative: points: hic 'this (here)', ille 'that (there)', is 'that / he', iste 'that of yours'
relative: quī, quae, quod 'who, which, that' — introduces a clause describing a noun
interrogative: asks a question: quis 'who?', quid 'what?', quī 'which?'
indefinite: someone / anyone / a certain one: aliquis, quisquam, quīdam, quisque
possessive: shows an owner: meus, tuus, suus, noster, vester
preposition: a little word before a noun telling its relation: in, ad, ab, cum. Each takes a fixed case
conjunction: joins words or clauses: et, sed, quia, ut
adverb: modifies a verb or adjective and never changes form: saepe, bene, nōn
numeral: a number word: ūnus (cardinal 'one'), prīmus (ordinal 'first'), singulī (distributive 'one each'), semel (adverb 'once')
indeclinable: never changes its ending (nihil, quattuor, frūgī)
principal parts: the forms you memorise for a verb: 1st person present, infinitive, perfect, supine/participle — mittō, mittere, mīsī, missum
stem: the unchanging part of a word that the endings attach to: labyrinth- in labyrinthō
ending: the changing tail of a word that carries case, number, person or tense: -ō in labyrinthō
citation form: how a dictionary lists a word: nominative + genitive for nouns, the principal parts for verbs
Greek declension: a borrowed Greek name keeping some Greek endings: Aenēās (acc. Aenēān), Thēseus (voc. Thēseu)
article: Latin has no 'a' or 'the' — add whichever English needs
postpositive: never stands first in its sentence: autem, enim, igitur, quidem come second
periphrastic: a form made of two words, like English 'is going to': missus est, mittendus est
ablative absolute: a noun + participle in the ablative standing apart from the sentence: 'Tacente Quīntō' = with Quintus silent / while Quintus was silent
indirect command: a command reported after a verb like 'order, ask, tell': imperat ut mittant = he orders that they send
purpose clause: ut / nē + subjunctive answering 'why?': vēnit ut vidēret = he came to see
result clause: ut / ut nōn + subjunctive answering 'so what happened?': tam fortis ut vinceret = so brave that he won
indirect question: a question reported inside a sentence, verb in the subjunctive: rogat quis sit = he asks who he is
sequence of tenses: a present/future main verb takes a present or perfect subjunctive; a past main verb takes an imperfect or pluperfect
